paragraphs: This paper examines how systems learn to locate visible sound sources using paired audio and video without bounding-box annotations. It identifies two problems in common evaluations: annotated data can still be used to decide when training stops, and evaluation metrics assume that a visible sound source is always present. These choices obscure both annotation costs and failures on scenes without visible sources.

The authors extend Flickr SoundNet and VGG-Sound Sources with negative examples containing no visible sound source. They evaluate methods using measures that balance localization accuracy and recall. Under this protocol, most earlier methods struggle to recognize negatives and depend heavily on early stopping to avoid overfitting.

The paper also introduces a localization approach using extreme visual dropout and momentum encoders. The authors report that these ingredients effectively reduce overfitting and achieve new state-of-the-art performance on both benchmarks. The contribution therefore combines a more revealing evaluation with a method designed to address the weaknesses it exposes.
neurips-2022-a-closer-look-at-weakly-sup.tldr: A revised audio-visual localization evaluation exposes overfitting and failures on negative examples, while a new method improves both benchmark results.

paragraphs: Active learning asks which unlabeled examples should receive labels next to improve a model most effectively. This paper approaches that choice through constrained learning. It places bounds on model performance for labeled examples, then jointly optimizes the model parameters and additional variables associated with those constraints.

These additional, or dual, variables describe how strongly changing a constraint would affect the best achievable objective. ALLY uses this sensitivity as a proxy for how informative an example is. It estimates dual variables for unlabeled examples and selects a diverse batch with high estimated values, connecting sample selection to the optimization problem used to train the model.

Experiments demonstrate benefits across classification and regression tasks. The paper also examines limitations associated with model capacity and redundant data, as well as the distribution shift introduced by actively choosing samples. Finally, it shows that ALLY can operate generatively, creating new samples intended to be maximally informative rather than selecting only from an existing pool.
neurips-2022-a-lagrangian-duality-approa.tldr: ALLY uses the sensitivity of a constrained learning objective to identify informative examples for labeling or generation.

paragraphs: Matrix completion reconstructs a low-rank matrix from observations of individual entries. At enormous scales, even operations on a full vector can be too expensive. Stochastic gradient descent is attractive because it supports inexpensive updates and streaming observations, including settings where the underlying matrix evolves. However, poor conditioning can dramatically slow its convergence.

The authors propose a preconditioned version of stochastic gradient descent that retains these practical advantages while removing dependence on the condition number from the stated convergence rate. For a symmetric target matrix and root mean square error loss, they prove that reaching error ε takes O(log(1/ε)) iterations, compared with the condition-number-dependent iteration requirement described for ordinary SGD.

This result makes the analyzed method converge as rapidly as if the target were perfectly conditioned. Numerical experiments also show acceleration for ill-conditioned matrix completion, Euclidean distance matrix completion, and collaborative filtering with their respective stated losses. Those experiments extend the practical evidence beyond the specific symmetric-matrix setting covered by the theorem.
neurips-2022-accelerating-sgd-for-highly.tldr: Preconditioned SGD removes condition-number dependence from a matrix-completion convergence guarantee while retaining suitability for huge streaming problems.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to learn predictors that remain reliable when test inputs are adversarially modified. It presents a learner that is minimax optimal: it achieves the best worst-case learning performance in the setting studied. Reaching this result requires a different algorithmic perspective from earlier approaches to robust learning.

The authors establish strong suboptimality results for an earlier robust learner and a broader family they call local learners. Their alternative takes a global view through a new mathematical construction, the global one-inclusion graph. This extends a classical tool for learning theory and enables the analysis behind the optimal learner.

A further result identifies a dimension that characterizes which predictor classes can be learned robustly and quantifies their sample requirements. This connects the possibility of robust learning with the amount of data it needs. The characterization resolves a previously open question and closes a gap between known upper and lower sample-complexity bounds that could potentially have been infinite.
neurips-2022-adversarially-robust-learni.tldr: A global graph construction enables minimax-optimal adversarially robust learning and a dimension characterizing robust learnability and sample complexity.

paragraphs: The paper investigates why adding neurons can make a neural network easier to optimize. Its setting is specific: a two-layer ReLU network trained with squared loss on labels generated by a target network. The analysis uses symmetries in this problem to examine undesirable local minima and how extra parameters change their surrounding loss geometry.

The authors derive precise estimates of loss values and Hessian spectra, which describe local curvature. They show that adding neurons can transform symmetric spurious minima into saddle points through a local mechanism that does not introduce new spurious minima. Minima with less symmetry require more added neurons for this transformation.

Using Cauchy's interlacing theorem, the analysis establishes directions of decreasing loss within particular symmetry-related subspaces. This gives a rigorous mechanism by which over-parameterization can help gradient-based optimization in the studied setting. For fixed numbers of neurons and inputs, the spectral conclusions also survive symmetry-breaking perturbations of the target, extending their relevance beyond an exactly symmetric target.
neurips-2022-annihilation-of-spurious-mi.tldr: Symmetry-based analysis shows how adding neurons can turn certain bad minima in two-layer ReLU networks into saddles.

paragraphs: The paper studies pricing when customer value depends linearly on observed context, but market noise has an unknown distribution. A pricing strategy must simultaneously earn revenue, estimate the linear valuation parameters, and learn that noise distribution without specifying a fixed parametric form. These objectives interact because the prices chosen also affect what the seller learns.

Explore-then-UCB separates part of this challenge into stages. It first explores to estimate the valuation parameters, then uses an upper-confidence-bound procedure to combine revenue seeking with learning the noise distribution. Under Lipschitz continuity and second-order smoothness of that distribution, its regret grows at rate T^(2/3), up to logarithmic factors.

With Lipschitz continuity alone, the method matches the best existing T^(3/4) regret rate while improving computational efficiency. The authors also establish a T^(3/5) lower bound, up to logarithmic factors, under the stronger smoothness assumptions. This supplies a benchmark for unavoidable difficulty, although the stated upper and lower rates do not coincide.
neurips-2022-contextual-dynamic-pricing-.tldr: Explore-then-UCB improves contextual pricing regret under smooth unknown noise and establishes a new lower bound for that setting.

paragraphs: CryptoGCN addresses private inference with graph convolutional networks using homomorphic encryption. This allows computation on encrypted data, but the required operations can be much more expensive than their unencrypted counterparts. The paper targets that overhead so graph-based prediction can become more practical in privacy-sensitive applications.

Its main technique organizes encrypted data around the graph's adjacency matrix. Adjacency Matrix-Aware formatting and patterned sparse matrix partitioning exploit sparse graph operations to reduce the number of homomorphic computations needed for matrix multiplication. A further co-optimization framework uses pruning and polynomial approximations of activation modules to explore trade-offs among accuracy, security level, and computational expense.

On the NTU-XVIEW skeleton joint dataset, the authors report up to a 3.10-fold latency speedup and a 77.4% reduction in homomorphic operation count compared with state-of-the-art solutions, with a stated accuracy loss of 1–1.5%. These results support the approach's efficiency on the evaluated workload while making its accuracy trade-off explicit.
neurips-2022-cryptogcn-fast-and-scalable.tldr: CryptoGCN exploits graph sparsity to accelerate encrypted inference, reporting up to 3.10-fold lower latency with a small accuracy loss.

paragraphs: Agents capable of solving many environments are often evaluated on a fixed collection designed by people. This paper studies automatic environment generation as a way to obtain collections that reveal varied agent behaviors. Quality diversity optimization is useful for this purpose because it seeks both high-quality environments and diversity in the behaviors they produce.

The computational difficulty is that evaluating each proposed environment may require an expensive agent simulation. Deep Surrogate Assisted Generation of Environments, or DSAGE, maintains a deep model that predicts how an agent will behave in new environments. This predictive surrogate supports a more sample-efficient search for useful and behaviorally diverse environment collections.

Across two benchmark domains, DSAGE significantly outperforms existing quality diversity environment-generation algorithms in discovering collections that elicit diverse behaviors. The evaluated agents include a state-of-the-art reinforcement learning agent and a planning agent. The findings support learned behavior prediction as a useful component of environment generation when repeated simulations are costly.
neurips-2022-deep-surrogate-assisted-gen.tldr: DSAGE predicts agent behavior with a deep surrogate to discover diverse environment collections more efficiently.

paragraphs: Snapshot spectral compressive imaging reconstructs a hyperspectral image from a compressed measurement. The paper focuses on deep unfolding methods, which organize learned reconstruction into iterative stages. It identifies two weaknesses in existing approaches: insufficient adaptation to the measurement's degradation and reconstruction difficulty, and limited ability to capture long-range relationships when relying mainly on convolutional networks.

The proposed Degradation-Aware Unfolding Framework estimates controlling parameters from the compressed image and physical mask. These parameters guide each reconstruction iteration. The authors also design a Half-Shuffle Transformer to capture local content together with dependencies between more distant parts of the signal.

Combining the framework and Transformer yields DAUHST, presented as the first Transformer-based deep unfolding method for this reconstruction task. Experiments report better reconstruction performance than state-of-the-art methods alongside lower computation and memory costs. The contribution links information about the measurement process with a model capable of representing both nearby and nonlocal relationships during iterative recovery.
neurips-2022-degradation-aware-unfolding.tldr: DAUHST combines degradation-aware iterative reconstruction with a Transformer, improving reported hyperspectral recovery while reducing computational and memory costs.

paragraphs: Learning several tasks together can help or hurt, so deciding which tasks should share training is consequential. Exhaustively testing groups becomes impractical because the number of combinations grows exponentially. This paper frames grouping as a prediction problem: estimate how much each task would gain from a proposed group compared with learning it alone.

The neural meta learner MTG-Net learns relationships between task combinations and their performance gains. The approach assumes that these relationships occupy low-dimensional manifolds despite the enormous combination space. An active learning strategy progressively chooses combinations for meta-training, aiming to obtain useful gain estimates from relatively few evaluated combinations.

Experiments across varied multi-task scenarios support the method's efficiency and effectiveness. In an evaluation with 27 tasks and more than one hundred million possible combinations, the method almost doubles the reported performance of the best existing solution at roughly the same computational cost. Its broader promise depends on whether the assumed learnable structure captures the relationships among task groups.
neurips-2022-efficient-and-effective-mul.tldr: MTG-Net learns to predict the benefits of task combinations, enabling effective multi-task grouping without evaluating every possible group.

paragraphs: This paper studies how shifting rewards changes learning in value-based deep reinforcement learning. Its central result connects a linear reward transformation with changing the initialization of the approximated Q-function. That equivalence gives a way to understand reward shifting through the value estimates that guide an agent's decisions.

The authors identify different effects for the direction of the shift. Positive reward shifting encourages conservative exploitation, while negative shifting encourages curiosity-driven exploration. They use the former to improve value estimation in offline learning and the latter to support exploration during online interaction. The same simple intervention therefore serves different purposes depending on how it is applied.

Experiments support these insights across several settings. Conservative exploitation improves offline performance with existing algorithms. In online continuous control, multiple value functions with different shift constants improve sample efficiency by addressing exploration and exploitation together. For discrete control, negative reward shifting improves a curiosity-based exploration method. These are reported task-level improvements, grounded in the proposed initialization equivalence.
neurips-2022-exploit-reward-shifting-in-.tldr: Reward shifts act like changes to Q-function initialization, supporting conservative offline learning or exploratory online learning depending on their sign.

paragraphs: The paper examines exploration in reinforcement learning when environments differ between episodes. It finds that several existing methods depend critically on an episodic count-based component of their exploration reward. Such methods can work well in simple, noise-free settings but struggle when the state space becomes large and observations contain noise.

Exploration via Elliptical Episodic Bonuses, or E3B, extends the idea of counting novelty to continuous state spaces. It encourages visits to states that are diverse within a learned representation during each episode. The representation is trained with an inverse dynamics model so that it captures aspects of the environment the agent can control.

E3B achieves new state-of-the-art results across 16 challenging MiniHack tasks without task-specific inductive biases. It also outperforms existing methods in reward-free exploration on Habitat. Together, these evaluations demonstrate effectiveness in the studied tasks and show that the approach can handle realistic environments with high-dimensional pixel observations, beyond the simpler settings motivating the analysis.
neurips-2022-exploration-via-elliptical-.tldr: E3B rewards within-episode diversity in learned controllable features, extending count-based exploration to continuous and visually complex environments.

paragraphs: This paper studies contextual bandits with the goal of identifying a good policy after collecting data. Given a policy class, the learner must return a policy whose expected reward is within ε of the best in that class, with probability greater than 1−δ. The focus is the number of samples needed for this guarantee.

The authors introduce an instance-dependent quantity, ρΠ, that characterizes this sample requirement. Matching upper and lower bounds are established for agnostic and linear contextual best-arm identification settings. Accounting for the particular problem instance makes the analysis sensitive to how difficult that instance is, rather than describing only worst-case difficulty.

The main algorithm achieves instance-optimal sample complexity and computational efficiency through a polynomial number of calls to a cost-sensitive classification oracle. The paper also proves that one algorithm cannot simultaneously attain the stated minimax optimality for regret minimization and instance-dependent PAC optimality for identification. This separates two objectives that might otherwise appear interchangeable in bandit learning.
neurips-2022-instance-optimal-pac-algori.tldr: The paper characterizes instance-dependent policy-identification complexity and gives an efficient optimal algorithm, separating this goal from regret minimization.

paragraphs: Stochastic differential equations incorporate noise into models of evolving systems, helping represent uncertainty and imprecise measurements. The paper argues that the idealized Brownian noise used in existing models does not cover the variety of noise characteristics encountered in real data. It develops a way to include generalized fractional white noise in neural differential-equation models.

A central computational contribution is an efficient approximation of noise sample paths. The method combines classical integration techniques with sparse Gaussian processes, providing a practical route to using the generalized noise formulation. This makes the noise model itself an adaptable part of the system being learned.

Experiments on time-series data show that the proposed model captures characteristics such as continuity and improves fitting compared with existing models. The authors also investigate its use in score-based generative models. They demonstrate a case where the generalized noise improves an image-generation measure, providing evidence for that application without claiming that every noise choice improves image generation.
neurips-2022-learning-fractional-white-n.tldr: Generalized fractional noise improves reported time-series fitting, with an efficient approximation and a demonstrated beneficial case for image generation.

paragraphs: Weak supervision combines noisy label estimates from accessible sources into pseudolabels for training. For binary classification, theory explains how estimating the noise can yield downstream guarantees close to those obtained with clean labels. This paper asks whether comparable guarantees extend to structured outputs, whose possible values have richer organization than ordinary class labels.

For labels in finite metric spaces, the authors introduce methods based on pseudo-Euclidean embeddings and tensor decompositions. These produce a nearly consistent estimator of label-noise rates. For labels on constant-curvature Riemannian manifolds, they develop invariants that support consistent noise-rate estimation. The mathematical tools differ to accommodate the structure of each output space.

In both settings, the resulting pseudolabels can be paired with a flexible downstream model to obtain generalization guarantees nearly matching clean-data training. The findings extend favorable weak-supervision theory to a wide range of structured prediction scenarios. They also provide robustness results about learning from noisy structured labels that may be useful beyond the specific supervision framework.
neurips-2022-lifting-weak-supervision-to.tldr: New noise-estimation tools extend near-clean-label generalization guarantees for weak supervision to several structured output spaces.

paragraphs: This paper brings perceptual inference and associative memory retrieval into a shared variational-inference formulation. Its central design makes the prior over latent representations depend on stored memories. As the system infers a representation, that prior draws the inference process toward representations encountered and stored previously.

Within this framework, the authors examine different neural approaches to carrying out inference. They compare amortized approaches, such as variational autoencoders, with iterative approaches, such as predictive coding. These offer different ways to obtain latent representations within the same memory-dependent formulation. The paper suggests combining the two approaches to construct new associative memory models.

The resulting algorithms are evaluated on CIFAR10 and CLEVR images and compared with Hopfield Networks, End-to-End Memory Networks, and Neural Turing Machines. These comparisons situate the proposed formulation among established memory architectures. The stated contribution is a unifying mathematical framework and an exploration of algorithms built from it; the abstract does not assert that one method wins those comparisons.
neurips-2022-on-the-relationship-between.tldr: A memory-dependent prior unifies perceptual inference and associative retrieval, enabling comparisons and combinations of amortized and iterative inference.

paragraphs: This paper investigates a form of posterior collapse encountered in Bayesian deep learning. It analyzes a general linear latent-variable model that includes linear variational autoencoders as a special case. This gives the authors a setting in which they can identify the mechanism precisely rather than merely observe that collapse occurs.

The identified cause is competition between the likelihood and the prior's regularization of the mean. These two parts of learning exert competing pressures: the likelihood concerns explaining the observations, while the prior contributes the regularization. The result locates the source of the studied collapse in their interaction, making the balance between them central to understanding the phenomenon.

Because the analyzed model contains linear variational autoencoders, the explanation applies beyond a single narrowly chosen linear architecture. The authors further suggest that posterior collapse may be a broader learning problem in deeper architectures. That extension remains a suggestion in the stated findings; the precise causal identification is established for the general linear model under study.
neurips-2022-posterior-collapse-of-a-lin.tldr: A linear latent-variable analysis attributes a form of posterior collapse to competition between likelihood fitting and prior-induced mean regularization.

paragraphs: Few-shot segmentation learns to segment new classes from very few labeled examples. A common strategy freezes the pretrained backbone to limit overfitting. This paper revisits that choice by allowing a small, carefully selected portion of the backbone to change, seeking adaptation without losing useful information learned during pretraining.

Singular Value Fine-tuning decomposes backbone parameters into three successive matrices using singular value decomposition. Training then changes only the singular values while keeping the other factors fixed. This restricted adjustment lets the representation respond to new classes while retaining semantic information in the pretrained backbone, offering a controlled way to fine-tune with scarce data.

The authors evaluate the approach across several few-shot segmentation methods and different backbones. They report state-of-the-art results on Pascal-5i and COCO-20i in both one-shot and five-shot settings. The findings support reconsidering complete backbone freezing: in these evaluations, adapting a small parameter subset improves generalization to new classes while addressing the overfitting concern that motivates freezing.
neurips-2022-singular-value-fine-tuning-.tldr: Fine-tuning only backbone singular values improves few-shot segmentation while preserving the remaining pretrained factors.

paragraphs: This paper studies stochastic gradient methods whose gradients are sampled through a Markov process. Earlier analyses largely examined whether these methods converge during optimization. The authors instead also ask how their learned solutions generalize, covering both minimization and minimax learning problems through algorithmic stability.

Their key tool is on-average argument stability, which tracks the average sensitivity of the learned solution to changes in training data. For empirical risk minimization, it yields optimal excess population-risk bounds in both smooth and nonsmooth cases. For minimax problems, the authors establish a quantitative relationship between this stability notion and generalization error, extending earlier results based on uniform stability.

The paper also derives nearly optimal convergence rates for convex-concave problems, both in expectation and with high probability. Combining those optimization results with stability establishes attainable optimal generalization bounds for smooth and nonsmooth cases. The contribution thus connects optimization progress with statistical performance when gradient samples have the dependence induced by a Markov process.
neurips-2022-stability-and-generalizatio.tldr: A stability analysis establishes generalization guarantees for stochastic gradient methods with Markov-dependent samples, including minimization and convex-concave minimax problems.

paragraphs: Uncertainty in a fitted predictive model also affects quantities computed from that model. The classical delta method propagates asymptotically normal model uncertainty through a differentiable evaluation, producing standard errors and confidence intervals. Applying it becomes difficult with complex models or evaluations, while bootstrap alternatives can be costly when training a model is already expensive.

The implicit delta method estimates downstream uncertainty by introducing an infinitesimal regularization into the training loss. It then examines how the downstream evaluation changes. This turns the response to a small training-objective perturbation into information about the variability of the evaluation estimator.

The authors prove that this change consistently estimates the evaluation's asymptotic variance, including when a finite difference approximates the infinitesimal perturbation. The result supports standard-error estimation and calibrated confidence intervals within the asymptotic framework. The paper also relates the method to Bayesian and frequentist uncertainty approaches and demonstrates it empirically, offering another route when direct uncertainty propagation is difficult.
neurips-2022-the-implicit-delta-method-7.tldr: The implicit delta method estimates downstream uncertainty from the response to a small regularization of a model's training loss.

paragraphs: Differential equations provide a useful language for studying neural-network training, even though gradient descent updates parameters in discrete steps. The paper addresses the discrepancy between those steps and continuous gradient flow. Its aim is a continuous description that more precisely captures the actual learning dynamics of gradient descent.

Starting from gradient flow, the authors derive a counter term that cancels discretization error and produces an equation of motion. They derive and solve this equation, while also analyzing discretization error to establish the extent of its precision. The correction therefore plays an explicit role in connecting the continuous model with the discrete update process.

The paper applies the equation to layers with scale invariance and translation invariance. These cases reveal differences between continuous and discrete gradient descent and show why the counter term matters for describing training dynamics. Experiments support the theoretical findings. The contribution is a more precise mathematical account of learning dynamics, accompanied by an analysis of its approximation accuracy.
neurips-2022-toward-equation-of-motion-f.tldr: A correction to gradient flow yields an equation of motion that captures discrete gradient-descent dynamics with explicitly analyzed discretization error.

paragraphs: Subpopulation shift occurs when training and test data contain the same groups but in different proportions. Importance weighting attempts to compensate by changing the influence of training examples. The paper addresses evidence that such weighting often fails to improve on ordinary empirical risk minimization, especially with over-parameterized neural networks.

Uncertainty-aware mixup, or UMIX, combines mixed training examples with uncertainty-based reweighting to mitigate overfitting. It estimates each example's uncertainty from its training trajectory and uses that information to weight the mixed samples. The trajectory-based estimates are intended to flexibly characterize the subpopulation distribution while guiding how strongly samples affect learning.

The authors provide theoretical analysis yielding better generalization bounds than prior work and empirical studies across a wide range of tasks. Those studies support the method's effectiveness both qualitatively and quantitatively. The contribution brings uncertainty estimation and mixup into importance weighting, addressing the interaction between distribution imbalance and overfitting rather than relying on sample weights alone.
neurips-2022-umix-improving-importance-w.tldr: UMIX reweights mixed training examples using trajectory-based uncertainty to improve generalization under subpopulation shift.

paragraphs: Batch normalization is widely useful in computer vision but often trails layer normalization in Transformer language tasks. This paper identifies inconsistency between batch normalization during training and inference as the leading cause of that weakness. It introduces Training Inference Discrepancy, or TID, to measure the mismatch quantitatively.

Experiments across image classification, machine translation, language modeling, sequence labeling, and text classification show that TID indicates batch normalization's performance. The authors find that batch normalization can substantially outperform layer normalization when this discrepancy stays small throughout training. This motivates directly controlling the mismatch rather than treating poor language-task performance as unavoidable.

Regularized Batch Normalization adds a regularization term that brings batch statistics closer to population statistics, suppressing growth in TID. It consistently improves batch normalization and matches or exceeds layer normalization in 17 of 20 evaluated settings, covering ten datasets and two Transformer variants. These results support discrepancy control as a practical remedy across the tested configurations.
neurips-2022-understanding-the-failure-o.tldr: Controlling batch normalization's training–inference mismatch improves Transformer performance, matching or beating layer normalization in 17 of 20 settings.

paragraphs: Mode collapse describes a lack of diversity in samples produced by generative adversarial networks. This paper introduces a particular geometric notion of diversity: how uniformly generated samples are distributed over the data manifold. It calls nonuniform coverage u-mode collapse and develops uniform diversity as a way to study that behavior.

The authors connect uniform diversity to a property of the generator itself, showing that a uniform generator achieves maximum uniform diversity. UniGAN pursues this property with a normalizing-flow-based generator and a sample-efficient regularization term. The regularizer is also presented as adaptable to other generative frameworks, giving the proposed objective a role beyond this architecture.

To evaluate the new notion in practice, the paper introduces udiv, a metric computed from generated samples. Experiments support UniGAN's ability to learn a uniform generator and improve uniform diversity. The findings concern this specifically defined form of sample coverage, providing a geometric perspective and corresponding training and evaluation tools for studying generative diversity.
neurips-2022-unigan-reducing-mode-collap.tldr: UniGAN targets uneven coverage of the data manifold through generator-uniformity regularization and a new diversity metric.

paragraphs: Vessels absent from conventional monitoring systems are difficult to track, complicating efforts to protect marine ecosystems. Satellite synthetic aperture radar offers observations by day or night and in all weather. However, radar imagery requires specialized handling, and maritime objects are small and sparse within large images, making automated detection challenging.

The paper introduces xView3-SAR, described as the largest labeled dataset for detecting and characterizing vessels and ocean structures in radar imagery. It contains nearly 1,000 analysis-ready Sentinel-1 images, averaging 29,400 by 24,400 pixels. Annotations combine automated and manual analysis, and every image includes geographically aligned bathymetry and wind-state rasters.

The authors also describe the international xView3 Computer Vision Challenge, which uses this resource for large-scale ship detection and characterization. Releasing the data and code gives researchers a shared basis for developing and evaluating methods. The contribution is an accessible, application-specific dataset and evaluation effort supporting automated identification of vessels that conventional monitoring may miss.
neurips-2022-xview3-sar-detecting-dark-f.tldr: xView3-SAR provides a large annotated satellite-radar dataset and challenge for detecting vessels missing from conventional monitoring.
